overview: This Senate resolution addresses a 1971 United Nations vote, Resolution 2758, that gave China's U.N. seat to the government in Beijing, the People's Republic of China, instead of the government on Taiwan. It says that vote settled only who represents China at the U.N. and did not decide Taiwan's political status, and that Beijing wrongly uses it to claim Taiwan belongs to China and to keep Taiwan out of international bodies such as the World Health Organization. It also explains that the U.S. "one China policy" only acknowledges Beijing's position, takes no stance on Taiwan's sovereignty, and differs from Beijing's "One China Principle." The resolution supports Taiwan's participation in international organizations, supports countries that keep ties with Taiwan, and says Taiwan passport holders should be able to enter U.N. grounds without Chinese-issued papers. As of April 28, 2025, the Senate Foreign Relations Committee had approved it and it was awaiting a vote by the full Senate.
for: Supporters say the resolution sets the record straight on a U.N. decision that Beijing misuses to isolate Taiwan and pressure other countries.
against: Critics say the resolution is a statement of opinion that does not change U.S. law, and it could raise tensions with China without giving Taiwan any concrete new support.
